notes: Long Munby judgment on publication in care proceedings; limited disclosure orders and section 12 analysis are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Re B: public debate and disclosure in MSBP care proceedings
key_facts: A mother in Kent care proceedings claimed miscarriage of justice after findings that she deliberately harmed her child, in the context of public concern following Sally Clark, Trupti Patel and Angela Cannings cases involving Sir Roy Meadow.

Bracewell J found the mother deliberately interfered with a hospital cannula and administered an unidentified substance causing rigors; Holman J made a final care order placing the child with paternal grandparents.
The mother sought leave to debate her case in public and to disclose expert reports and judgments to the GMC and the wider public.
The mother and her solicitor Ms Sarah Harman had already disclosed confidential court material, giving rise to contempt concerns and ex parte injunction applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for leave to disclose family court documents and to publish specified matters into the public domain, following earlier contra mundum anonymity orders.
enrichment.outcome: Limited leave granted to disclose specified documents to the GMC and certain edited matters into the public domain; contra mundum anonymity order maintained; mother accepted undertakings restraining wider publication.
enrichment.ratio: Section 12 of the Administration of Justice Act 1960 protects privacy and confidentiality of documents on the court file and of what occurs in court, but does not prevent all public discussion of proceedings; leave may be granted for narrowly defined disclosure where justified, but unauthorised dissemination of protected material amounts to contempt; the court must balance open justice against the welfare of the child and frankness of family proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the mother may debate her case in public
Scope of section 12 restrictions on publication in family proceedings
Whether leave should be granted to disclose expert reports and judgments to the GMC
Whether prior unauthorised disclosures constituted contempt of court

Re B (a Minor) [2003] EWHC 20 (Fam)
Re L (A Minor) (Wardship: Freedom of Publication) [1988] 1 All ER 418

confidence.notes: Core publication law analysis and final disclosure orders are clear. Child and expert identities are anonymised in the judgment, limiting detail on some factual findings.

notes: Supporting Link public-interest winding-up petition; grounds on misrepresentation and charity regulations clearly established.

enrichment.short_title: Supporting Link: public-interest winding up of telesales publisher
key_facts: Supporting Link Alliance Ltd sold advertising space in regional business guides by cold-calling small businesses, emphasising charitable donations and local distribution.
The Secretary of State presented a public-interest winding-up petition after a section 447 investigation by DTI officers.
The company was solvent but used fake debt-collection letters, misrepresented distribution areas, and used charity logos without proper consent.
Director Mr Simister offered undertakings to reform trading practices; the Secretary of State opposed accepting undertakings instead of winding up.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Hearing of Secretary of State's petition to wind up Supporting Link Alliance Ltd on just and equitable grounds in the public interest.
enrichment.outcome: Compulsory winding-up order made; undertakings refused; grounds relating to misrepresentation, charity regulation breaches and unauthorised logo use established.
enrichment.ratio: Where a company carried on business founded on deliberate deception as to charitable contributions, regional editions and distribution, it is just and equitable to wind it up on a public-interest petition; the court should be very slow to dismiss such a petition on undertakings unless the Secretary of State consents, because policing undertakings is not the Department's function.
legal_issues: Whether Annual Business Guides were directories under the Unsolicited Goods and Services Act 1971
Whether breaches of charity fundraising regulations justified winding up
Whether regional distribution and charity representations were materially misleading
Whether undertakings offered by the company should be accepted instead of a winding-up order
linked_authorities: Re Walter L Jacob Ltd [1989] 5 BCC 244
Re Bamford Publishers Ltd (2 June 1977, unreported)
Re Blackspur Group Plc [1998] 1 WLR 422
Re Senator Hanseatische [1997] 1 WLR 515

confidence.notes: Findings on trading practices, statutory grounds and refusal of undertakings are detailed and explicit in the judgment.

notes: Licensing costs judicial review; Totnes Justices principles applied and case stated directed rather than quashing.

enrichment.short_title: Police costs order in licensing application judicial review
key_facts: Lancashire Constabulary objected to Mr Cairns's justices' on-licence application for the Netherfield Club on fitness grounds.
Magistrates granted the licence and ordered the Chief Constable to pay Mr Cairns's costs of £2,015.56.
The police argued the costs order was Wednesbury unreasonable because the objection was made in good faith performing a statutory licensing function.
Magistrates refused to state a case; the Chief Constable sought judicial review to quash the costs order or direct a case to be stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of magistrates' costs order in licensing proceedings and refusal to state a case.
enrichment.outcome: Application to quash the costs order refused; magistrates directed to state a case to the High Court; costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Costs in licensing objections are discretionary; where police perform a statutory licensing function in good faith, an adverse costs order should not be made merely because the applicant succeeded, but may be made where the objection was without foundation or improper; on short reasons it was unfair to quash without a stated case for fuller argument.
legal_issues: Whether the magistrates' costs order was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether time for applying for a case stated ran from the costs assessment date
Whether police licensing objections attract special protection on costs
Whether magistrates should state a case on the costs order

notes: Obasa EAT adjournment refusal; Article 6 fair hearing analysis and permission refusal are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Obasa: refusal to adjourn EAT disability discrimination appeal
key_facts: Miss Obasa, a Northamptonshire County Council employee with sickle cell disease and dyslexia, brought race and disability discrimination claims that largely failed in the employment tribunal.
After multiple adjournments due to counsel non-attendance, the EAT refused her request to adjourn a narrow appeal heard without representation on 17 July 2003.
Judge Levy allowed a short adjournment for her to review papers but proceeded and dismissed the appeal on the merits.
Miss Obasa applied to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal alleging procedural unfairness and breach of Article 6.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against Employment Appeal Tribunal refusal to adjourn and dismissal of disability discrimination appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; transcript of oral judgment ordered at public expense.
enrichment.ratio: Refusal of an adjournment is a discretionary case-management decision reviewable only if abhorrent to fairness; where the appeal point was narrow, the appellant was familiar with her case and effectively presented it, and delays had already burdened the respondent, Article 6 was not breached by proceeding without counsel.
legal_issues: Whether the EAT's refusal to adjourn was procedurally unfair
Whether Miss Obasa was denied effective access to court under Article 6
Whether the appellate court should overturn a discretionary adjournment decision
Whether litigant in person with dyslexia required representation to present the appeal
linked_authorities: Hadmore Productions v Hamilton [1983] 1 AC 191
Airey v Ireland [1979] 2 EHRR 305
X v United Kingdom [1984] 6 EHRR 136
McVicar v United Kingdom [2002] 25 EHRR 22

confidence.notes: Adjournment reasoning, Article 6 analysis and permission refusal are explicit in Potter LJ's judgment.

notes: Burridge Oman cycling accident; contributory negligence appeal dismissed after inadequate trial reasons but Court of Appeal decided issue.

enrichment.short_title: Burridge: contributory negligence in Oman minibus door collision
key_facts: Mr Burridge, cycling on a hard shoulder in Muscat, Oman, collided with the off-side door of a minibus that had pulled onto the shoulder.
The driver Abdul Ghafoor opened the door without checking mirrors; Burridge was knocked into the path of another vehicle and suffered severe injuries.
Liability was established at trial; the recorder found no contributory negligence but gave inadequate reasons.
The defendants appealed only on contributory negligence, arguing a cyclist should have anticipated the door opening.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against county court finding of no contributory negligence in liability-only trial of overseas road traffic accident claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; recorder's contributory negligence decision set aside for inadequate reasons but Court of Appeal found no contributory negligence; defendants ordered to pay appeal costs of £24,917.25.
enrichment.ratio: A driver who opens a door without looking is primarily liable; it is not enough that a stationary minibus on a hard shoulder made door-opening foreseeable in a general sense; without evidence that a reasonably careful cyclist should have moved into fast traffic or stopped, contributory negligence cannot be established merely because the cyclist overtook a parked vehicle.
legal_issues: Whether the recorder gave adequate reasons on contributory negligence
Whether a cyclist should have anticipated the driver's door opening
Whether Burridge had opportunity to take evasive action
Whether the Court of Appeal could determine contributory negligence without retrial

Lewis v Denye [1939] 1 KB 540

notes: Seretide patent revocation for obviousness; Ventide common general knowledge analysis is detailed and conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Seretide patent revoked for obvious combination inhaler
key_facts: Four generic pharmaceutical companies sought revocation of Glaxo's UK patent 2,235,627 covering a combined inhaler of salmeterol and fluticasone propionate (Seretide/Advair).
The only issue at trial was obviousness of combining a beta-2 agonist and inhaled steroid in one inhaler at the priority date.
Glaxo's earlier Ventide product combining salbutamol and beclomethasone in one inhaler was part of the skilled person's common general knowledge.
Glaxo senior manager Dr Rapeport improperly pressured expert Professor Page before trial; contempt referral was considered but not pursued.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated trial of four revocation actions against Glaxo Group Limited's asthma combination inhaler patent.
enrichment.outcome: Patent held invalid for obviousness; claim 1 found to be obvious therapy at the priority date; Dr Rapeport apologised but contempt referral declined.
enrichment.ratio: Where the skilled person knew combined beta-2 agonist and steroid inhalers such as Ventide and salmeterol was part of common general knowledge, combining salmeterol with fluticasone in a single inhaler at the priority date was obvious; subsequent commercial success of Seretide does not establish non-obviousness.
legal_issues: Whether claim 1 of patent 2,235,627 was obvious at the priority date
Whether Ventide formed part of the common general knowledge
Whether salmeterol's pre-clinical status prevented an obvious combination
Whether Glaxo's conduct towards expert witnesses amounted to contempt
linked_authorities: Windsurfing International Inc v Tabur Marine (Great Britain) Ltd [1985] RPC 59
Pozzoli Spa v BDMO SA [2007] EWCA Civ 588

confidence.notes: Obviousness conclusion on claim 1 is explicit and central. Some citation-based invalidity arguments were subsidiary to the Ventide analysis.

notes: BCCI Morris v Bank of India; s.213 knowing participation and $43.231m contribution quantified.

enrichment.short_title: Bank of India liable for BCCI fraudulent window-dressing transactions
key_facts: Between 1981 and 1986 Bank of India entered six year-end transactions with BCCI under which BCCI deposited funds and BOI lent equivalent sums to BCCI-nominated borrowers.
The arrangements window-dressed BCCI's accounts to improve its earnings-to-advances ratio and conceal bad debts; BCCI's fraud is admitted.
BCCI liquidators alleged BOI knowingly participated in carrying on BCCI's business with intent to defraud creditors.
Mr Samant, BOI's senior London manager, was found to have known the transactions assisted BCCI's fraudulent concealment of losses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by BCCI liquidators for contribution under section 213 of the Insolvency Act 1986 against Bank of India.
enrichment.outcome: BOI held liable to contribute to creditor losses; payment ordered of US $43.231 million with interest from liquidation at base rate plus 1% unless further argued.
enrichment.ratio: Knowledge of a senior manager authorised to negotiate and implement transactions is attributable to the bank; where window-dressing transactions were intended to mislead auditors and readers of accounts, participation amounts to knowing assistance in a fraudulent purpose even if the bank believed the practice assisted legitimate accounting presentation; section 213 permits interest on the contribution.
legal_issues: Whether BOI knowingly participated in BCCI's fraudulent business
Whether Mr Samant's knowledge was sufficient to fix BOI with liability
Quantum of contribution to creditor losses avoided but for the transactions
Whether interest should be awarded on a section 213 contribution

notes: Executor account summons under section 25; permission to appeal out of time granted for costs challenge.

enrichment.short_title: Executor account summons and permission to appeal out of time
key_facts: Mr N S, executor of his father's 1983 will, failed for years to provide a full estate account to his sister beneficiary C I.
Probate was granted in August 1984 on an estate sworn at £88,750; the beneficiary received nothing under the will and suspected under-accounting.
After correspondence from 1999, partial accounts in 2003 showed a deficiency of about £19,600 which did not satisfy the claimant.
The registrar ordered verified inventory and account and assessed costs at £5,140 in the executor's absence; the executor later sought to set aside the order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside registrar's order for estate inventory and account under section 25 Administration of Estates Act 1925, with appeal out of time.
enrichment.outcome: Application properly brought in non-contentious probate jurisdiction; permission to appeal out of time granted so executor could challenge costs and raise laches.
enrichment.ratio: A personal representative has a statutory duty to exhibit a full inventory and account when required by the court; a beneficiary's request for information under section 25 is a proper non-contentious probate step before any administration action; delay is a discretionary factor but does not extinguish the duty; an absent party may be granted permission to appeal out of time when not fully heard.
legal_issues: Whether the summons was properly issued in non-contentious probate proceedings
Whether a Part 8 claim in the Chancery Division was required
Whether the registrar had jurisdiction to order an account and costs
Whether permission to appeal out of time should be granted

confidence.notes: Jurisdiction analysis and permission to appeal grant are clear. Merits of the account dispute and laches defence were not finally determined.

notes: Sevenoaks golf course condition 12 enforcement appeal; no implied implementation obligation and costs upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Golf course condition 12: no implied compliance obligation
key_facts: Outline permission for a 27-hole golf course at Pedham Place was granted in 1990 subject to condition 12 requiring engineering work details to be submitted and approved before commencement.
Earth bunds were built between two and 5.89 metres higher than approved engineering details.
Sevenoaks District Council issued enforcement notice B alleging breach of condition 12; the developer appealed.
The Inspector quashed the notice, holding condition 12 did not require works to be carried out in accordance with approved details, and awarded costs against the council.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 289 appeal against planning inspector's decision allowing enforcement appeal and awarding costs to the developer.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; enforcement notice correctly quashed; inspector's costs order against the council upheld; Secretary of State's costs assessed at £4,565.50.
enrichment.ratio: A planning condition requiring prior approval of details is clear on its face and does not implicitly require implementation in accordance with those details; breach of planning control by non-compliance with a condition cannot be founded on an implied obligation; implied conditions are not permissible in planning permissions; Circular 11/95 warns that approval-only conditions may not be enforceable for implementation.
legal_issues: Whether condition 12 impliedly required engineering works to match approved details
Whether bund height deviations breached planning control
Whether planning conditions may be construed to include implied implementation obligations
Whether the inspector reasonably awarded costs against the local planning authority

notes: Petros harassment injunction appeal; consent order and hopeless permission applications dismissed in absentia.

enrichment.short_title: Petros doctors: harassment injunction consent and hopeless appeals
key_facts: Sunaina Chaudhari, born with fatal Edwards Syndrome, died aged five months at King George's Hospital after doctors declined intensive care.
Her mother Mrs Chaudhari alleged murder and organ theft, campaigning outside hospitals and online against six doctors and a pathologist.
The doctors obtained summary judgment and struck out the mother's counterclaim; Mrs Chaudhari gave undertakings by consent on 21 October 2003.
She continued publishing allegations online; doctors sought to enforce undertakings while Mrs Chaudhari applied late to appeal the consent order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications for permission to appeal consent orders and Pitchers J directions, heard in defendants' absence before Chadwick LJ.
enrichment.outcome: Both permission applications dismissed as hopeless and out of time; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: There is no basis to appeal a consent order adjourning claims where undertakings were given through counsel; late applications without explanation should be refused; directions on refusal of rights of audience and fixing trial dates are routine case management not amenable to appeal; breach of undertakings should be enforced in the High Court rather than by appealing the consent order.
legal_issues: Whether consent order giving undertakings could be appealed out of time
Whether Pitchers J's case management directions were appealable
Whether Dr Adoco should have rights of audience
Whether undertakings restraining harassment should be enforced

confidence.notes: Procedural history, consent undertakings and dismissal of hopeless appeals are clearly narrated by Chadwick LJ.
